title: Gothic classification, transmission and independent development
question: Which similarities among European cathedrals belong to broad stylistic classification, which follow chronology and program, and which support a specific transmission of architectural practice?
selection_rationale: The four prescribed corpus Features are joined by Amiens because the Cologne dossier names it directly. The set yields two Feature-level transmissions, one explicit technical limiter, a mixed-style Canterbury case and a Romanesque Santiago boundary without converting chronology into causality.

features.name: Chartres Cathedral
features.selection_rationale: Provides a documented early-thirteenth-century formula and the UNESCO statement that its fundamental design was imitated at Cologne.

features.name: Amiens Cathedral
features.selection_rationale: Adds the one permitted Feature because the Cologne nomination specifically distinguishes adoption of Amiens artistic components from its technical innovations.

features.name: Cologne Cathedral
features.selection_rationale: Offers two source-named French references and a long construction history that prevents dates alone from being mistaken for a single causal event.

features.name: Canterbury Cathedral
features.selection_rationale: Supplies a building with Romanesque, early Gothic and later Gothic phases plus a documented transfer of expertise from Sens.

features.name: Santiago de Compostela Cathedral
features.selection_rationale: Acts as the classification stress case: the cathedral is a Romanesque masterpiece inside an urban ensemble that also contains Gothic and Baroque work.

sources.title: ICOMOS Evaluation: Cologne Cathedral No. 292rev
sources.publisher: ICOMOS via UNESCO World Heritage Centre

sources.title: Canterbury Cathedral, St Augustine's Abbey, and St Martin's Church

claims.statement: Chartres established an early-thirteenth-century architectural formula that became a major reference for later Gothic work.
claims.uncertainty: A broadly influential formula does not establish a separate pairwise Relation to every later Gothic cathedral.

claims.statement: UNESCO states that the fundamental design of Chartres was imitated in Cologne.
claims.uncertainty: The heritage statement does not enumerate the exact design components or route of transmission.

relation.qualifier: fundamental design at an unspecified component level

claims.statement: UNESCO describes Amiens Cathedral as an important influence on the later development of Gothic architecture.
claims.uncertainty: UNESCO's general influence statement does not by itself identify Cologne as a recipient.

claims.statement: The ICOMOS evaluation judges that Cologne's master builder Gerhard appears to have incorporated artistic components from Amiens into the new cathedral.
claims.uncertainty: The evaluation says Gerhard was familiar with several French cathedrals and emphasizes Amiens, so the relation is selective rather than exclusive.

relation.qualifier: artistic components, with other French precedents also in view

claims.statement: The Cologne evaluation explicitly says Gerhard did not incorporate Amiens's technical innovations.
claims.uncertainty: The evaluation does not list the excluded technical innovations, so the boundary needs specialist architectural review.

claims.statement: Canterbury Cathedral is stylistically heterogeneous, combining Romanesque fabric with early and later Gothic campaigns.
claims.uncertainty: A building-level classification must preserve phase and component qualifiers instead of assigning one undifferentiated style.

claims.statement: After the 1174 fire, the French master mason William of Sens brought new building techniques and a different architectural style to Canterbury.
claims.uncertainty: The official learning page does not enumerate the techniques or define the style more narrowly, so this remains a contextual Claim rather than a counted pairwise Relation.

claims.statement: UNESCO classifies Santiago's cathedral as a Romanesque masterpiece.
claims.uncertainty: The cathedral includes later interventions, including a Baroque western façade, so the assertion is about the core monument classification rather than every visible element.

classification_assertion.qualifier: later interventions and the surrounding urban ensemble span other styles

claims.statement: Offerings from large numbers of pilgrims helped finance Canterbury's east-end enlargement and post-1174 rebuilding.
claims.uncertainty: The UNESCO passage establishes a financial contribution, not a single cause for every formal decision.

claims.statement: The influx of pilgrims to the relics of the Magi helped motivate Cologne's decision to replace its Romanesque cathedral with a larger building.
claims.uncertainty: The ICOMOS history also records archiepiscopal ambition, so pilgrimage demand was an important factor rather than the sole cause.

conclusion.statement: The evidence distinguishes a broad Gothic classification from two source-named transmissions into Cologne: modelling on Chartres's fundamental design and an ICOMOS judgment that Gerhard appears to have selectively adapted Amiens artistic components. The Amiens technical limiter, Canterbury's phased fabric and Santiago's Romanesque core show why neither shared style nor chronological order can substitute for a qualified RelationClaim.

module_uncertainty: The component meaning of Chartres's “fundamental design” requires specialist review.
The ICOMOS phrase “artistic components” is not granular enough to identify every Cologne element.
William of Sens supplies contextual evidence of French expertise reaching Canterbury but is not represented as a counted pairwise Relation.
Santiago's later fabric must remain visible when applying a Romanesque classification to the core cathedral.
Claims and EvidenceLinks remain draft until both independent reviewers confirm the corrected frozen revision.
